newsitem.title: UK: POLL-UK UNEMPLOYMENT TO DROP, EARNINGS SEEN STEADY.
newsitem.headline: POLL-UK UNEMPLOYMENT TO DROP, EARNINGS SEEN STEADY.

text.p: Britain's dwindling jobless queues are expected to have shrunk by a further 31,000 in July, continuing a long-established trend of falling unemployment, according to a Reuter poll of economists.

And perhaps more importantly for the financial markets, the poll of economists found the majority expected underlying annual average earnings growth to stick fast at 4.25 percent in June, despite an ever-tightening labour market.
The figures are due at 0830 GMT on Wednesday.

Michael Saunders, Salomon Brothers' UK economist, said survey evidence of firms' recruitment intentions remains strong and suggests unemployment will continue to fall steadily over the next few months.
"The jobless rate is already within a whisker of the 5.6 percent low seen at the end of the 1980s boom and is likely to hit that mark in the July figures," he said.

The jobless rate, which dropped to 5.7 percent in June, reached a trough at 5.6 in May 1990. Unemployment has been tumbling fast for more than a year. In July last year, the overall rate stood at 7.6 percent.
The main concern for markets is that that rate of job creation will force wages higher and fuel inflation as available labour becomes scarcer.
But average earnings growth dropped from 4.5 percent to 4.25 in May, a fall which Marian Bell, UK economist at the Royal Bank of Scotland, said took the markets aback.

"With the labour market tightening further, the upward pressure on average earnings remains but it is unlikely, unless there is a significant rise in wage settlements, that underlying average earnings growth will have picked up in June," she said.
Bell forecast a 20,000 fall in unemployment. A drop of that magnitude pales in comparison with monthly falls of 60,000 plus seen earlier this year.
But those hefty reductions were due in part to a jobseekers' allowance, which was introduced to replace old-style unemployment benefit and led to a huge backlog in claims.
Ciaran Barr, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said the distortions of the allowance had now dropped out of the claimant count, revealing a still-strong underlying trend in job creation.
"With employment expectations remaining strong in the surveys, we expect unemployment to decline in the near term by around 30,000 each month," he said.
The Reuter poll forecast unit wage costs, which measure pay increases compared with productivity, will have risen by 2.6 percent in the three months to June, up from 2.4 percent in May.

"With a small fall in manufacturing output on a three-month basis and no signs of layoffs or pay cuts in the manufacturing sector, it should be no real surprise that we are forecasting unit wage costs to rise in the three months ending in June," Bell said.
